title: Detect Remote Access via USB Hardware (TinyPilot, PiKVM)
shortTitle: Detect Remote Access via USB Hardware (TinyPilot, PiKVM)
summary: This strategy detects hardware based remote access, where a small computer such as a TinyPilot or a PiKVM is attached to a target machine over its video and USB ports and then driven from a web browser anywhere on the network. The covered technique matters because the device impersonates a keyboard and a screen, so it needs no software agent, writes no commands into the operating system, and survives a full reinstall of the host. Host device connection telemetry and USB hub inventory make it detectable, because a new human interface device or video capture device appears at the moment of attachment. The main failure mode is that the operating system logs a device arrival but not the cable, so the rule depends on knowing which USB devices each site expects and on correlating the event with a physical inspection.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for a small spy computer plugged into a machine's video and USB ports. The device pretends to be a keyboard and a screen. It lets somebody outside the room control the machine as if they were sitting there.
beginner.whyItMatters: Software agents can be removed, but this device leaves nothing on the disk. It works even when the machine is locked, and it keeps working after the operating system is reinstalled. Because it types like a real keyboard, ordinary login controls may trust it. Only the hardware connection gives it away.
howItWorks: The operating system logs each new device the moment it is attached to a port.
A remote access device appears as a keyboard, a mouse or a video capture device.
The detection watches for those device classes arriving on server or kiosk hosts.
It compares the new device against an inventory of hardware each site normally uses.
It also looks for device arrivals outside working hours or on locked consoles.
An analyst then asks somebody on site to inspect the physical ports.
beginner.example: Imagine a night watchman who trusts anyone wearing the company uniform. A stranger walks in with a uniform and a clipboard, stands at the front desk, and signs the visitor book on the guard's behalf. Nothing in the building changed, and the visitor book looks tidy, but an outsider is now doing the work.
takeaways: Hardware remote access leaves no software trace, so watch the device connection itself.
Keep a written inventory of approved USB devices for sensitive machines.
Treat any new keyboard or video capture device on a server as a physical security event.

objectives: Describe how a keyboard and video capture appliance provides remote control without software.
Recognise which device classes indicate a new human interface or video capture device.
Compare device arrival events against an approved hardware inventory for each site.
Combine device telemetry with physical access records and maintenance schedules.
Explain why disk based investigation and reimaging do not remove this kind of access.
dataSources: Windows plug and play device installation events recording new USB human interface devices and video capture devices with vendor and product identifiers
Linux kernel device manager logs recording newly attached USB devices including class, vendor identifier and product identifier
Endpoint management or asset inventory records listing approved USB peripherals per host and site
Physical access control records and visitor logs for the server room or data centre housing the host
logic: The pattern is a new human interface device or video capture device appearing on a host that does not normally accept removable peripherals, especially outside maintenance hours or while no interactive user is logged on. The telemetry is the operating system device installation log, plus kernel device manager records on Linux, and the fields that must be correlated are the device class, the vendor and product identifiers, the serial number, the port or hub, the host name and the event time. Benign behaviour is a keyboard replacement or a console crash cart attached during a scheduled maintenance window on a host whose inventory already lists that model. Malicious behaviour is a keyboard plus video capture pair arriving together on a rack server or an attended kiosk, from a vendor the site has never used, at a time with no maintenance record and no logged on user, or on many hosts in sequence as somebody walks the racks. The pairing of an input device with a video capture device on the same host in the same short window is the strongest single indicator, because a real technician rarely needs both at once from unknown hardware.
pseudoQuery:
# title: New USB keyboard and video capture device on a server host
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: system
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventSource: 'Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-PnP'
#     DeviceClass:
#       - 'HIDClass'
#       - 'Image'
#   filter_approved:
#     DeviceId|in: approved_usb_inventory
#   condition: selection and not filter_approved
# level: medium
falsePositives: Break glass crash cart keyboards and monitors stored in the data centre and attached during an incident
Hardware maintenance where a technician replaces a faulty keyboard or adds a capture card for video wall testing
Kiosk or digital signage hosts that receive a new approved capture device as part of a refresh project
Lab and test benches where engineers attach capture hardware to record boot sequences or firmware output
Video conferencing endpoints that install a capture device when a meeting room system is upgraded
tuningNotes: Build the approved device inventory from thirty days of normal device arrival events per host group and key exclusions on the vendor and product identifier plus serial number rather than on the device name alone, because cheap adapters share generic names. Scope the alert tightly to rack servers, hypervisors, domain controllers and kiosks, and raise severity when an input device and a capture device arrive on the same host within a short window or when no user session is active. Accept that scoping loses coverage on ordinary workstations, so keep a separate low severity rule there and review it alongside physical access records. Re-check the allow list after every hardware refresh, and add a periodic report of devices attached outside business hours so slow or repeated visits stay visible.
